claims.text: Synchronizing the reduction kinetics of multiple noble-metal precursors enables simultaneous nucleation.
Simultaneous nucleation yields uniform high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Simultaneous nucleation produces a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Sequential or unsynchronized reduction causes phase separation.
Sequential or unsynchronized reduction causes heterogeneous nanoparticle morphologies.
Phase separation and heterogeneous morphologies reduce the exposure of catalytically active surface sites.
Stabilizing agents can ensure comparable dispersion of the different metals in the precursor mixture.
A suitably tuned thermal treatment can synchronize the reduction kinetics of all metal precursors.
A controlled atmosphere and temperature–time profile minimize differences in metal-precursor reactivity.
Transient nucleation clusters form during synchronized reduction.
Transient nucleation clusters promote atomic-level mixing of the metal species.
Staggered reduction leads to sequential nucleation and elemental segregation.
A synchronized reduction regime will produce more homogeneous alloys than conventional uncontrolled thermal treatment.
A synchronized reduction regime will produce greater surface-atom exposure than conventional uncontrolled thermal treatment.
A synchronized reduction regime will improve catalytic performance relative to conventional uncontrolled thermal treatment.
Standard thermal treatments that do not specifically control reduction kinetics often produce staggered reduction rates.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy systems containing five or more components when surface-atom exposure is important.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to non-noble-metal-dominated compositions or systems in which specialized precursor chemistry overrides reduction kinetics.
Catalytic activity can serve as an indirect measure of surface-atom exposure.
